sources.news_title: Trump to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy: Stop striking Russian diesel refineries
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Sunday said he told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian refineries, claiming they are “causing a shortage of diesel.”
“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said to reporters. “…We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel.”
Trump added that the diesel shortage “isn’t done by the Middle East.”
“This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” Trump said.

While Ukraine has been attacking Russia’s oil and gas industry, leading the latter to ban diesel exports until the end of September, the U.S. war against Iran has also affected the diesel supply and prices. Renewed conflict in Yemen has also raised the risk premium on global oil flows.
On Friday, oil prices were at over $100 a barrel — Brent crude oil futures were $104.61 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate was $100.05.
Diesel prices this past week set an all-time high of $6 per gallon on average across the U.S. In California, some stations even set the sticker price for diesel at $9.99 — some to indicate that they were out of the fuel.
Net exports of diesel/gasoil from the Gulf countries averaged 390 kb/d in August as the Strait of Hormuz stays restricted amid the Iran conflict, according to the International Energy Agency. That’s just over a quarter of what exports were before the war.
“Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the IEA said. “Combined, net exports of diesel/gasoil exports from the Gulf and Russia in August were 1.6 mb/d lower than in February, when they accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade.”
Because of the U.S.-Iran war and attacks in the Gulf and the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb choke point, the IEA cut its supply and demand projections for the rest of 2026.
“With buffers shrinking and the global refining system stretched to the limit, the need for progress in resolving the conflict in the Middle East — and the Russia-Ukraine war, which is now in its fifth year — is greater than ever to avoid further market tightening and demand destruction,” the IEA said.
Russian drone strikes train on Ukraine-Poland border
A Russian drone struck a train at the Ukraine-Poland border on Sunday, shortly after a different train carrying several European officials, including former United Kingdom Prime Minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, passed by, Ukrainian Railways (Ukrzaliznytsia) said on Telegram.
A dispatcher from the Central Monitoring Group detected the drone, and a signal to evacuate the train was issued 15 minutes before it landed. There have been no reports of casualties.
“It is highly likely that the Russian drone’s intended target was actually the diplomatic train, which had departed the station earlier than scheduled due to real-time timetable adjustments necessitated by the constant threat of Russian strikes,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding that it “continuously adjusts train schedules based on which routes are available and which are blocked due to attacks.”
Another train carrying former CIA Director David Petraeus was still at Yahodyn station when the attack happened, Ukrzaliznytsia said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned “Russia’s barbaric strikes.”
“This is Putin’s terror “knocking” directly on the doors of the [European Union] and NATO,” he said. “Act now: throw the full weight of your sanctions at [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s aggressive regime.”
Johnson said the strike is “the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day — even on civilian railways.”
“I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning,” he said.
Bildt posted a video of the attack on X and said “No one was hurt.”
“Very good safety system,” he said. “Our train just had an evacuation warning but could proceed to Dorohusk.”
A gas station was also damaged in the drone strike, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Along with Ukrzaliznytsia, energy facilities, businesses, and ordinary residential buildings were attacked Saturday night and Sunday morning, Zelenskyy said.
“Odesa was attacked with missiles and drones. Recovery efforts are ongoing in many western regions following the overnight strikes,” he said. “It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand.”
At least nine people were hurt in the overnight attack on Odesa, Serhii Lysak, of the city’s military administration, said, according to The Associated Press. A separate Russian drone attack hit a residential high-rise in Odesa on Saturday, the AP reported. Two people were killed and another 26 wounded.
Ukrainian forces targeted oil refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai and the Republic of Tatarstan, the Kyiv Independent reported Sunday, with fires breaking out at both facilities. Two people were killed in Tatarstan, and 12 were injured, regional authorities said.
Two Russian civilians in Nizhnekamsk died when a drone slammed into a tree near their car, the office of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov said.

sources.news_title: Trump Urges Zelenskyy to Halt Strikes on Russian Diesel as Fuel Shortage Deepens
sources.text:
President Donald Trump urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks are contributing to fuel shortages as Russia and Ukraine continue exchanging large-scale drone strikes.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian diesel infrastructure, arguing that Ukraine’s campaign against refineries is contributing to fuel shortages inside Russia.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf club in Ireland, Trump was asked whether he had spoken with Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters.
“Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel.”
Ukraine has spent months using long-range drones to strike Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities, arguing that the industry both finances Moscow’s war and supplies fuel used by Russian forces. The campaign has disrupted production and contributed to fuel rationing despite Russia’s status as a major global oil and gas producer.
Trump’s remarks came as both countries carried out another major exchange of drone attacks overnight into Sunday.
Ukraine said it struck a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Russia’s Krasnodar region, with the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine saying drones hit a key processing unit and the refinery’s tank farm. Russian regional authorities acknowledged that an attack on an industrial facility injured three people, damaged an oil pipeline and started a fire, although they did not directly confirm Ukraine’s description of the target.
The latest round of strikes also reached Russia’s Tatarstan region, where two people were killed and 14 others injured near the industrial city of Nizhnekamsk.
Russian officials said a Ukrainian drone struck a tree near a parked vehicle, killing two civilians. Nizhnekamsk contains a major concentration of Russian oil refining, petrochemical, rubber and polymer facilities, while Mayor Radmir Belyaev reported that a fire had broken out at an unspecified enterprise.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night.
Russia simultaneously launched hundreds of drones against Ukraine, with Kyiv saying Moscow deployed 453 unmanned aircraft of various types overnight. Ukraine’s air force said its defenses shot down or suppressed 409 of them, including newer jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept.
At least nine people were injured during what officials described as a “massive” Russian attack on Odesa, Ukraine’s principal Black Sea port.
The assault followed another drone strike Saturday that hit a residential high-rise in Odesa, killing two people and injuring 26 others. Russia has increasingly targeted Ukrainian cities, power infrastructure and transportation networks in recent weeks as winter approaches, while Ukraine has continued directing strikes at Russia’s energy industry. (CBS News)
Western Ukraine also came under attack, including an area close to the Polish border.
A Russian drone struck near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland and ignited a fire near a petrol station. Ukrainian authorities said the crossing itself remained intact and no one was injured.
“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X.
The border area is strategically important because crossings between Poland and Ukraine serve as major routes for Western military equipment and humanitarian assistance entering the country.
Earlier in the week, two people were killed when Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk separately said a “direct threat” to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point had been avoided through cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv. Tusk did not provide further details or evidence directly attributing that incident to Russia.
The escalating strikes are unfolding as Washington, Moscow and Kyiv again explore the possibility of negotiations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Sunday that Russia would not rule out restarting talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States as early as October.
“We are not ruling out that possibility. We are specifically talking about the foreseeable future. That is, October cannot be ruled out,” Peskov told reporters.
Ukraine has also indicated that preparations are underway for another possible round of negotiations.
Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s presidential office, said Kyiv was preparing for potential trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States, although no location has been announced.
The renewed diplomatic effort follows recent meetings by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who met Putin in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv for discussions with Zelenskyy.
Despite the latest diplomatic contacts, Russia and Ukraine remain divided over the central conditions for ending the war, particularly questions involving territory.
Trump’s comments introduce another issue into those negotiations by calling specifically for Ukraine to stop damaging Russia’s diesel supply while allowing Kyiv to continue striking other targets.
Ukraine has treated Russia’s oil and refining network as a strategic vulnerability, arguing that reducing fuel production places financial and logistical pressure on Moscow.
Trump, however, is now publicly drawing a distinction between those energy strikes and other Ukrainian military targets.
“Let him go after targets,” Trump said, “but not diesel fuel.”

sources.news_title: President Donald Trump calls on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel, saying attacks causing a shortage
sources.text:
KYIV, Ukraine — U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the U.S. hit a record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average.
Ukraine has for months been targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry with long-range strikes, prompting fuel rationing across the country and causing Moscow to ban diesel exports in July, removing supplies from the already tight global market.
But the global crunch also came after the war on Iran curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in midterm elections in November.
Trump was asked by a reporter if he had spoken with Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He responded by calling on Zelenskyy to halt strikes against Russia.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open, which is being played at his Doonbeg golf club.
“We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world,” he said.
Diesel exports from Gulf countries way down since Iran war began
According to a report published Friday by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf countries in August stood at “just over a quarter” of what they were before the war on Iran began in February.
“Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the IEA wrote. It added that in February, combined next exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf and Russia “accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade.”
Kyiv says Russia’s oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow’s more than four-year-old invasion of Ukraine.
Russia has ramped up its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce Ukraine’s defenses. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralize civilians.
Civilians were killed and injured overnight into Sunday as Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone strikes.
Two people were killed and 14 more wounded near an oil and industrial hub in Russia’s Tatarstan, according to local officials, while Ukrainian authorities reported on Russian drones pummeling the Black Sea port of Odesa and starting a fire near a border crossing with Poland.
Ukraine targets more Russian oil facilities
The two Russian civilians died after a drone slammed into a tree near their parked car in the city of Nizhnekamsk, according to the office of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov. Nizhnekamsk houses a key cluster of oil refineries and other industrial plants. Mayor Radmir Belyaev said that a fire had broken out at an unspecified “enterprise.”
Ukraine also claimed to have hit a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, in Russia’s Krasnodar region near Crimea. The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) agency said its drones struck a key oil processing unit and the refinery’s tank farm overnight into Sunday.
Krasnodar authorities said the strike on “an enterprise” in Slavyansk-on-Kuban injured three people and damaged an oil pipeline.
Russian forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night, Russia’s defense ministry said Sunday.
Russia targets Odesa and western Ukraine
In Ukraine, at least nine people were injured in a “massive” Russian nighttime attack on Odesa, according to Serhii Lysak from the city’s military administration. Odesa is home to Ukraine’s main port hub on the Black Sea and has faced sustained drone and missile strikes, with Kyiv accusing Moscow of trying to choke off its exports.
A Russian drone attack on Saturday struck a residential high-rise in Odesa, killing two people and injuring 26 others, Ukrainian officials said.
Russian overnight strikes also pounded western Ukraine, though there were no immediate reports of casualties. One drone set fire to a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland, according to Ukraine’s top diplomat and a spokesperson for the local customs force.
“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X.
Ukraine’s border crossings with Poland are a conduit for much of the military and humanitarian aid sent by Western allies.
Valentyna Chernysh, a spokesperson for the Volyn Customs Office, told The Associated Press that the Yahodyn crossing was intact and no one was harmed.
Earlier this week, two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday. The following day a “direct threat” to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point was avoided due to the cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, according to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
Ukraine’s air force said its air defenses shot down or suppressed 409 Russian drones of various types overnight, including a newer jet-powered version that is faster and more difficult to intercept. It said Russia had attacked Ukraine with 453 drones in total.

sources.text:
Trump’s visit to Ireland has seen the American leader again fusing his brand of off-the-cuff diplomacy with both his love of golf and private businesses.
On Saturday, he caught his Irish hosts and the neighbouring UK off-guard when he waded into highly sensitive political territory by announcing he would “love to see” a united Ireland.
‘Not welcome here’ 
Breaking with Washington’s traditional neutrality on the historically charged topic, Trump argued reunification of the Republic of Ireland and UK territory Northern Ireland – after more than a century apart – was “going to happen eventually”.
“It may as well happen now,” he said as he met Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, prompting pushback from pro-UK loyalists in Northern Ireland and some leading politicians in mainland Britain.
Trump doubled down on his remarks Sunday.
“I’m someone who owns fantastic property here,” he said after watching Irish Open leader Shane Lowry tee off in the final round on the Trump Organisation course bought in 2014.
“It would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together,” he added, insisting “many people agree”.
Trump arrived in Doonbeg on Saturday afternoon, sparking road closures and police checkpoints nearby. Around 30 people protested his visit in neighbouring Doonbeg village on Sunday.
“Donald Trump is not welcome in Ireland,” demonstrator William Hederman, 53, told AFP, accusing him of helping Israel commit genocide in Gaza.
Trump’s attendance at the tournament added an extra layer of complexity to a security effort that is reportedly costing Ireland €20 million ($23 million). He is expected to present the winner with the trophy later on Sunday.
Spectators cheered when he walked on to the first tee.
“It’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” 28-year-old Connor McGovern, who had travelled from Northern Ireland hoping to see the President, told AFP.
‘Conflict of interest’ 
The former real estate magnate, who promotes his enterprises at every opportunity, was joined in the remote corner of Ireland by his two sons, Eric and Don Jr.
They have managed the family business since their 80-year-old father returned to the White House last year.
The course – set among dunes on the rugged County Clare coastline – has twice been targeted by pro-Palestinian activists in the past 18 months.
Police said three women – aged in their 20s, 30s and 40s – had appeared in a western Irish court late on Saturday after being arrested for separate trespass and public order offences there.
Around 4000 Irish and US security personnel were involved in the weekend-long security operation, with anti-drone technology among the measures deployed.
The golf-mad President plays golf most weekends at one of his family’s US properties.
He is scheduled to host December’s G20 summit at his Miami golfing resort.
Opposition Democrats in the US have long complained that blurring the lines between his presidency and personal business interests is corrupt.
The White House has aggressively pushed back against claims of conflicts of interest and that Trump has been using his presidency to enrich himself as his personal wealth has rocketed during his second term.
“Since the Civil War, we haven’t had a president with a significant financial conflict of interest from a business enterprise,” University of Minnesota Law School professor Richard Painter told AFP.
The former White House ethics lawyer warned that Trump’s conduct could send the message “that the way to curry a favour with the President is to patronise his properties, do business with his companies and so forth”.
- AFP

By being thankful for the small things every day, we are far more likely to be and stay healthy so that we can enjoy them.

Express your needs
People need consistency and connection to feel safe. This is not, ‘You hurt my feelings by never replying to me’, it’s more ‘this is the kind of contact that helps me feel secure’.

If a relationship repeatedly inflames your nervous system, you need to disengage and deprioritise it.

Will Harlow, a physiotherapist for the over-50s and author of Independence for Life, shares the key signs you’re ageing badly – and what to do about it.
Ageing well is maintaining the ability to do what you want you want for as long as you want without needing help. Everyone is talking about longevity but what’s the point in living longer if the last decade is painful and you’re [totally] reliant on people?”
The signs to look out for
The most obvious early warning sign of bad ageing is pain says Harlow.
Another is losing confidence in doing daily tasks, which can quickly lead to a lack of independence.
One call Harlow often receives is people calling after having a fall and struggling to get up.
When people retire, they often put their feet up and stop. Your body really is use it or lose it.
Sleep
Throughout our entire lives, Harlow says we need between seven and nine hours of sleep.
Social isolation
The lack of connection can increase the risk of premature death by as much as 29 per cent.
Strength training
It really is the proxy for overall independence.
The more muscle mass you have, the less chance of heart disease, diabetes, falls and even anxiety, depression and dementia.
The brain can be linked to muscle mass too, Harlow says. It’s not just about being able to lift things. It gives you more energy, better sleep and you’ll look and feel better.
How to age without pain
Daily habits
Do short bursts of exercise, between 30 and 60 seconds, in otherwise dead time during the day.
Stretch in bed
Take joints through a full range of motion for five minutes to loosen it before getting up.
Don’t crash diet
It can increase the decline of muscle mass and bone density, which needs to be avoided.
How to age without pain
Protein
Harlow advises 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight to stop muscle loss alongside resistance training.
Don’t wait
Harlow finds that many patients put off making a change to their lifestyle until their lives are consumed by pain.
Recovery
For most people, it’s about reducing the number of times per week you’re exercising, not reducing intensity.
The three ageing tests to do
Lie completely flat on the floor and get back up to a standing position using any technique. This should take less than 10 seconds.
See how many times you can sit on the chair and stand back up again in 30 seconds. Men should be aiming for more than 14 times and women 12.

Never mind that the US’s war against Iran caused the spike in diesel and petrol prices, or that Ukraine is fighting for its life against Vladimir Putin’s forces. In Trump’s mind, the quick solution to diesel prices hitting $6 a gallon at home appears to be to blame a country that is supposed to be an ally and was invaded by a foreign aggressor.
The sudden concern for the welfare of the planet wasn’t a sign that he is changing – it was a reminder of his own rampant self-interest. It is also a sign of how desperate the President has become ahead of what is expected to be a harsh rebuke from voters in the US midterm elections in November.
Faced with dismal poll numbers, this week Trump resorted to claiming Americans would get a $5,000 dividend if Republicans kept control of Congress, a move that was deemed possibly illegal, and so expensive his party baulked at the $1trn price tag.
Trump knows his war in the Middle East is to blame for higher fuel prices and for inflation refusing to go down. He has repeatedly tried to end the conflict, but so far to little avail. But he would never admit that he is responsible, so he has looked around for somebody else to blame – and seemingly settled on Ukraine.
Presidential trips to Ireland are about as easy as it gets: during Barack Obama’s 2011 visit locals joked about his Irish roots and gave him the nickname “O’Bama”. Joe Biden loved visiting the country as he can trace his ancestry there.
Yet Trump’s comments about Ukraine were the second diplomatic hand grenade he threw during what should have been a quiet weekend of golf watching.
Trump’s visit, which coincided with the Irish Open at the Trump International resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, was essentially a golfing weekend dressed up as diplomacy. But on Saturday he told Micheál Martin, Ireland’s Taoiseach, that he would “love” to see Ireland unified.
Breaking with decades of precedent since the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, which ended the Troubles, Trump said that unification would “happen eventually”.
The comment sparked surprise and outrage, including from Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, who said that Northern Ireland being part of the UK was the “settled democratic will of its people”.
Two weeks ago, Andy Burnham said a referendum on the reunification of Ireland was “off the table” but Trump seemed to be unaware of those comments, or just didn’t care.
Taken with his words about Zelensky and Ukraine, it was yet another sign that Trump cares little about the impact his words will have on US allies.
Despite this, the White House is likely to view his trip as a success, simply because of what didn’t happen. The President did not start any new wars, outright attack any close ally or capture the head of any other foreign states. There was also less AI slop going out on his social media account and he didn’t have time to start another row with Mark Carney, the Prime Minister of Canada, with whom he has engaged in a trade war.
It also helped that, in the US, most TV news stations and publications were preoccupied with the threat of an AI apocalypse – and the efforts of the industry to slow development of its most advanced models.
If anything, Trump’s inner circle will relish what they will see as a win from the two-day trip: mocking the EU and leaving a firestorm in the President’s wake.
That’s the upside-down logic of the Trump administration, and a reminder of why it is so hard to deal with the President. Who knows if what he said about Ukraine was serious, or if he really meant it about the reunification of Ireland. There rarely appears to be a strategy beyond what comes out of Trump’s mouth in the moment, and no deep and well-considered plan for international relations.
Come Monday, he will be back in the US and Ireland can breathe a somewhat sigh of relief. But someone else will likely be the next target of the human wrecking ball in the White House.

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the U.S. hit a record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average.
Ukraine has for months been targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry with long-range strikes, prompting fuel rationing across the country and causing Moscow to ban diesel exports in July, removing supplies from the already tight global market.
But the global crunch also came after the war on Iran curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in midterm elections in November.
Trump was asked by a reporter if he had spoken with Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He responded by calling on Zelenskyy to halt strikes against Russia.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open, which is being played at his Doonbeg golf club.
“We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world,” he said.
Diesel exports from Gulf countries way down since Iran war began
According to a report published Friday by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf countries in August stood at “just over a quarter” of what they were before the war on Iran began in February.
“Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the IEA wrote. It added that in February, combined next exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf and Russia “accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade.”
Kyiv says Russia's oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow's more than four-year-old invasion of Ukraine.
Russia has ramped up its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce Ukraine’s defenses. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralize civilians.
Civilians were killed and injured overnight into Sunday as Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone strikes.
Two people were killed and 14 more wounded near an oil and industrial hub in Russia’s Tatarstan, according to local officials, while Ukrainian authorities reported on Russian drones pummeling the Black Sea port of Odesa and starting a fire near a border crossing with Poland.
Ukraine targets more Russian oil facilities
The two Russian civilians died after a drone slammed into a tree near their parked car in the city of Nizhnekamsk, according to the office of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov. Nizhnekamsk houses a key cluster of oil refineries and other industrial plants. Mayor Radmir Belyaev said that a fire had broken out at an unspecified “enterprise.”
Ukraine also claimed to have hit a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, in Russia’s Krasnodar region near Crimea. The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) agency said its drones struck a key oil processing unit and the refinery’s tank farm overnight into Sunday.
Krasnodar authorities said the strike on “an enterprise” in Slavyansk-on-Kuban injured three people and damaged an oil pipeline.
Russian forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night, Russia’s defense ministry said Sunday.

In Ukraine, at least nine people were injured in a “massive” Russian nighttime attack on Odesa, according to Serhii Lysak from the city's military administration. “This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X.
Ukraine’s border crossings with Poland are a conduit for much of the military and humanitarian aid sent by Western allies.
Valentyna Chernysh, a spokesperson for the Volyn Customs Office, told The Associated Press that the Yahodyn crossing was intact and no one was harmed.

DOONBEG, Ireland — U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian oil refineries in light of the surging price of diesel fuel worldwide.

Asked about the current surge in global fuel prices, particularly diesel — which broke a record $6 per gallon in the U.S. on Friday — Trump insisted the spike was being caused by Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran, which has sharply restricted oil shipments from the Middle East.

DOONBEG, Ireland, Sept 13 (Reuters) – U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks were causing a shortage of the fuel that is “hurting the world”.
A wave of long-distance Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in recent months has reduced that country’s fuel production, triggering gasoline shortages across the country.

Trump tells Ukraine to stop targeting Russia’s diesel as Kyiv says Moscow attacked passenger train near Polish border
By Sophie Tanno and Daria Tarasova-Markina, CNN
(CNN) — US President Donald Trump has urged his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to stop targeting Russia’s diesel fuel in aerial attacks, claiming that it is “hurting the world.”
A series of long-distance Ukrainian drone strikes has targeted Russia’s fuel infrastructure, hitting major processing plants and significantly reducing its refining capacity.
“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia. Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said during an official visit to Ireland on Sunday.
“This isn’t done by the Middle East. This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” he claimed.
His comments come as the ongoing war with Iran, which predominantly involves the United States, Iran and Israel, has caused global energy prices to surge. The crisis has particularly affected traffic through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint.
Global oil prices rose to $108 this week as fighting in the Middle East raises concerns about prolonged supply disruptions. US diesel prices have hit record highs, topping $6 a gallon Friday for the first time ever.
Russia is the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel, behind the US, according to marine intelligence firm Kpler.
Attacks near Polish border
Meanwhile both Russia and Ukraine are continuing to escalate their air war, with a Russian drone attack overnight into Sunday hitting a gas station in the northwest Ukrainian town of Yahodyn near the country’s border with Poland, Ukrainian authorities said.
Attacks on gas stations have become so common that one Ukrainian network has started installing mesh cages around its facilities in the capital, Kyiv, to reduce the impact zone during strikes.
The latest attack drew swift response from Ukraine. Condemning the actions of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X: “Russia’s barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border crossing point in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders. This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO.”
The border crossing was briefly shut but was operating normally again by 10 a.m. local time Sunday.
Yahodyn is one of several Ukrainian-Polish border crossings through which a significant amount of Western military and humanitarian aid is delivered to Ukraine.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, speaking in Kyiv on Sunday, warned of the wider implications of Russian attacks close to Poland’s border.
“Russia carried out the attack using upgraded drones equipped with jet engines and improved guidance systems. This is an escalation. It is another major challenge for Ukraine, but also for the potential future victims of Russian aggression,” Sikorski said.
Ukrainian Railways said the locomotive of a passenger train was also struck by a Russian drone two kilometers from the Polish border. Ukrainian Railways said that shortly before the attack on that train, a diplomatic train at Yahodyn station had on board security advisers from several European Union member states and former European leaders, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson.
Another train at Yahodyn station at the exact moment of the attack was carrying former CIA director David Petraeus, it said.
Ukrainian Railways said that while it was still clarifying details, it is “quite likely” that the Russian drone could have deliberately targeted the train carrying diplomats. It added that the train “departed the station earlier than scheduled as part of real-time adjustments to train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes.”
“I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning,” Johnson said in a post. “What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day – even on civilian railways.”
Johnson said Russia had been responsible for the deaths of hundreds of Ukrainian Railways employees since its 2022 full-scale invasion and praised the rail workers and their passengers as “absolutely heroic.”
The former prime minister of Sweden, Carl Bildt, said he was on a train near the Polish border when a train behind his was targeted by a Russian drone. Bildt had been attending an international security conference in Kyiv known as the Yalta European Strategy (YES).
“This wasn’t our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing,” Bildt wrote on X alongside a video appearing to show a drone hitting a nearby train as throngs of passengers evacuate.
Zelensky said that in the past week alone, Russia had fired more than 2,000 drones at Ukraine, many of them jet-powered models, which are faster and more difficult to intercept than regular drones.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces continued targeting railway infrastructure in the west of Ukraine on Sunday. “Strikes continued against railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that are used to transport military cargoes from European countries,” Russian state news agency TASS reported, citing a statement from the ministry.
Strike inside Russia
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military said it had struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Tatarstan republic overnight into Sunday.
Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces said that it struck the TANECO refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, in an attack carried out alongside the Security Service of Ukraine and the Main Intelligence Directorate.
Tatarstan officials said two civilians were killed and others injured in a Ukrainian attack on Nizhnekamsk.
NATO countries, particularly Ukraine’s neighbors, are on high alert for military drones straying into their airspace.
On Sunday, Lithuania said that a perceived drone sighting in its airspace prompted authorities to close Vilnius airport and NATO to scramble at least one fighter jet.
The air alert was later lifted after the NATO jet identified the sighting as birds, Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center said. A similar alert in Poland last week also turned out to have been triggered by birds.

US President Donald Trump has called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure amid Russia's relentless attacks across Ukraine, including near the Polish border.
"There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel," Trump told reporters on September 13 during his visit to Ireland. "You have to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," he said.
Trump's comment came a week after his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, had visited Kyiv and Moscow in the latest US-mediated diplomatic effort to bring the wartime capitals closer to a negotiated agreement.
While all sides have called the talks "substantial," the dynamics on the front line have not changed, with Russia continuing to attack Ukraine and hitting its civilian, logistics, and energy infrastructure as the cold weather sets in.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued to respond, targeting energy and military sites inside Russia with its long-range drone attacks. Kyiv has been calling the effort "long-range sanctions" as it seeks to curb Moscow's energy profits and force it to negotiate.
Since the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian drone strikes have caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia and stoked discontent among its citizens, who were disconnected from the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine Warns Russia 'Knocking On NATO's Door'
With the latest diplomatic efforts yielding no practical easing of tensions on the battlefield, two Russian drone strikes hit near the Polish border early on September 13.
The first strike hit a petrol station near the Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine, in the latter's Volyn region. No casualties were reported.
The second, also in Volyn, struck the locomotive of a passenger train just two kilometers from the Polish border, Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, reported. According to Oleksandr Shevchenko, a local transportation official, the train was traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw.
As Ukrzaliznytsia said that a threat-monitoring group was able to warn the train's crew of the attack in advance, no casualties were reported. Video footage spread over Ukrainian social media showed people running from the blast at the railway station.
Separately, Ukrzaliznytsia said that "quite possibly," the original target of the drone strike could have been the "diplomatic train," which carried top European officials, including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson. It added that former CIA Director David Petraeus was aboard another train at the time.
As the incidents occurred, air-raid alerts were issued in several eastern districts of Poland.
While there were no reports of violations of Polish airspace, Jacek Goryszewski, spokesman for the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces, said the "threat to Poland was real."
In separate incidents on September 13, Romanian authorities reported a drone entering the country, and Lithuania called on residents in the capital and neighboring regions to preventively seek shelter after issuing an alert of possible drone sighting.
The country's main airport in Vilnius was shut down and NATO jets were scrambled. The alert was called off within an hour.
"Russia's barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X on September 13. "This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO."
He urged European leaders to "throw the full weight" of sanctions against Russia.
Earlier this month, Germany officially blamed an incident on Moscow in which explosive-laden drones interrupted flights at Leipzig Airport. At the time, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europeans are faced with a hard truth that this is the new normal."
"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every single day, laying down their lives to keep this aggression from expanding," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram on September 13.
"Russian terrorism is a shared threat to many, but it can and must be defeated right here in Ukraine," he added.
According to Zelenskyy, a total of 2,100 drones, 1,700 gliding bombs, and 73 missiles were launched at targets across Ukraine in the past week.
Ukrainian authorities said that elsewhere in Ukraine, the latest Russian attacks had also targeted the country's western regions of Ivano-Frankivsk, Ternopil, and Lviv, as well as the war-torn eastern Donetsk region and the key southern region of Odesa.
Regional authorities in the Odesa region said nine people had been injured after a drone struck several residential buildings. A warehouse in the region was also reportedly targeted.
Meanwhile, in the region's capital city of Odesa, rescuers have completed work at the site of the drone strike on a 25-story residential building on the night of September 12. Two people were killed and more than 20 injured in that attack.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that its overnight strikes targeted "logistics centers through which military cargo is delivered and distributed, as well as energy facilities that support their operation."
The ministry also reported strikes on railway infrastructure in western Ukraine.
Russia denies targeting civilian areas despite widespread evidence of such attacks that have killed thousands of people since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.

sources.news_title: Trump urges Zelenskiy to halt strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to stop attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure, arguing that the strikes were contributing to a fuel shortage affecting the global economy.
Trump made the remarks while attending the Irish Open golf tournament in Ireland. He said the disruption was “hurting the world,” placing public pressure on Kyiv over a campaign Ukraine says is directed at facilities that support Russia’s war effort.
Ukraine has repeatedly used long-range drones against Russian refineries and other energy assets. Kyiv describes such sites as legitimate military targets because refined fuels supply Russian armed forces and because Moscow continues to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Russia has reported disruptions to refinery operations and fuel availability after successive Ukrainian attacks. The effect of individual strikes varies, and damaged units can sometimes return to operation after repairs. However, repeated attacks can reduce processing capacity, complicate logistics and force operators to adjust production.
Trump linked the campaign to high diesel prices outside the conflict zone. The national U.S. average had risen above $6 per gallon, according to the reporting available on Sunday. Diesel costs are especially important to freight transport, agriculture and other sectors that rely on heavy vehicles and machinery.
The U.S. president’s intervention highlights a tension between Ukraine’s military objective of reducing Russia’s capacity to sustain the war and wider concern about energy-market consequences. It did not amount to an announced change in U.S. military support, and the available reporting did not include an immediate public response from Zelenskiy.
Moscow has reduced its oil-output forecast and revised expectations for fuel exports through 2027. Those changes reflect a combination of wartime damage, operational constraints and market conditions. The precise contribution of Ukrainian strikes to global diesel prices remains difficult to isolate from other supply disruptions.
Trump’s request was specific to diesel infrastructure. He did not announce a broader agreement with Kyiv on targeting policy, and there was no indication in the initial report that Ukraine had committed to halt its operations.
Further clarity will depend on any response from the Ukrainian government and whether Washington raises the issue through formal bilateral channels.
GasBuddy data cited by Reuters showed the U.S. national diesel average moved above $6 a gallon for the first time on Thursday. Trump said he had already discussed the refinery campaign with Zelenskiy and argued that Ukraine had other targets available. Reuters did not report the date, format or outcome of that conversation.
Russia’s draft government forecast, reviewed by Reuters, lowered the country’s 2026 oil-output expectation to its weakest level in 17 years and revised projected fuel exports for 2026 and 2027. A draft forecast can still change before formal adoption, so its figures should be treated as the government’s working assumptions rather than final production data.

Trump Calls on Zelenskyy to End Strikes on Russian Fuel Infrastructure
Reporting by CBS News and the Associated Press, President Donald Trump on Sunday urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russia's diesel supply, arguing the campaign is worsening a global fuel shortage.
Trump made the remarks on the sidelines of the Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf club in Ireland.
Trump told reporters that Zelenskyy should leave Russia's diesel facilities alone, saying there are other targets to pursue.
He also said he had already spoken with Zelenskyy directly on the matter, urging him not to strike fuel infrastructure because it is hurting the wider world beyond Russia.
Ukraine's Rationale for the Strikes
Ukraine has maintained for months that Russia's oil and gas industry directly finances and physically fuels its invasion, now in its fifth year.
6abc reported that the Ukrainian drone campaign has caused fuel rationing inside Russia, a notable development given that the country is one of the world's major oil and gas exporters.
On Sunday, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence agency claimed its drones struck a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Russia's Krasnodar region, hitting a key processing unit and the refinery's storage tanks and sparking a large blaze.
Krasnodar regional authorities confirmed a fire at an unspecified facility there, saying three people were injured and an oil pipeline was damaged.
Overnight Drone Attacks Kill Civilians
The back-and-forth struck civilians on both sides overnight.
Two people died in Nizhnekamsk, a city in Russia's Tatarstan region home to major oil refineries and petrochemical plants, after a Ukrainian drone struck a tree next to their parked car.
Fourteen more were injured in the same area, according to regional officials cited by CBS News.
Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa was hit hard: at least nine people were injured in a large Russian drone attack overnight into Sunday, and a separate Russian strike the previous night on a residential high-rise killed two people and injured 26 others.
Russian drones also struck western Ukraine, with one drone hitting near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland, setting fire to a petrol station.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the strike placed Russian military action directly at the edge of European Union and NATO territory.
The crossing itself was not damaged and no one at the site was harmed, a Ukrainian customs spokesperson told the Associated Press.
Russia's defense ministry said its forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russian regions and Russian-occupied Crimea.
Kremlin Open to Autumn Peace Talks
On the diplomatic front, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow is not ruling out renewed peace negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States as soon as October, according to CBS News.
Last weekend, U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and then with Zelenskyy in Kyiv.
Core territorial disputes between the two sides remain unresolved.
